title: A fuel cycle with substantially stronger built-in proliferation resistance

concept.text: The innovation would be a complete civilian nuclear fuel cycle designed to make acquiring nuclear material for weapons substantially harder and more detectable. Its scope includes material flows, processing facilities, transport, storage, disposal and the interfaces through which inspectors verify civilian use. The advance would have to emerge from the architecture as a whole: a favorable material property or an individual facility feature would not, by itself, establish substantially stronger resistance across the cycle.

Built-in, or intrinsic, features are properties of materials, processes and facilities that impede misuse or help make it observable. They must work alongside extrinsic measures such as safeguards, verification arrangements and institutional controls. Civilian cycles can contain weapons-usable material or material that could become weapons-usable after further processing. Assessment therefore needs to consider diversion, misuse of declared facilities and the potential use of civilian technology in undeclared activities, under explicit threat assumptions.

significance.text: A practical architecture demonstrating large, durable improvements could be an enabling systems advance for civilian nuclear energy. Greater difficulty of misuse could reduce opportunities to acquire material, while better detectability could strengthen deterrence and create opportunities for a response. The benefit would depend on demonstrating these gains across credible pathways throughout the lifecycle, rather than improving one attribute while leaving an easier route elsewhere.

Conditional synthesis: if the gains proved substantial, affordable and deployable, the architecture could improve the conditions for verified civilian nuclear use and confidence in its expansion. The revolutionary scale of the result would depend on the magnitude and robustness of the improvement and the resources needed to sustain verification. The supplied evidence does not quantify those benefits or establish that such an architecture has achieved them.

Stronger intrinsic resistance would not make proliferation impossible, prevent an independent weapons programme or eliminate the need for international cooperation. A material or process barrier cannot be assumed to defeat every pathway. Even intrinsic detectability has practical value only when safeguards and security systems can observe the relevant materials and activities. State cooperation, transparency, institutional effectiveness and available resources would remain consequential.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in the proposed innovation is an integrated, economically credible cycle that delivers substantially stronger resistance under defined threats while retaining workable civilian operations. Establishing that capability requires tracking material and technology across the complete system and showing that improvements at one stage do not simply displace vulnerability to another. The supplied record establishes this design and assessment challenge; it does not establish the latest demonstration status of every candidate architecture.

A concrete engineering barrier is the interaction among protective features. Multiple barriers do not necessarily provide independent protection: an action that defeats one can also defeat others. Material properties, processing difficulty, facility design and observability must therefore be assessed together, including alternative routes and facility misuse. A comparison must also recognize that different cycles can have different vulnerabilities; neither the presence of civilian material of concern nor a favorable individual attribute establishes an overall ranking.

Verification presents a further practical barrier. Safeguards must be able to use the architecture's observable features, and assessments must document their evidence, uncertainties, verification arrangements and costs. Proposed engineering priorities include demonstrating detection performance under representative operating conditions, accounting for measurement uncertainty, and resolving tradeoffs with safety, security and operational practicality. Those priorities are a synthesis of the assessment problem, not evidence that a particular design has resolved it.

current_state.text: The November 2008 INPRO Manual—Proliferation Resistance, Volume 5, documents a framework for evaluating innovative nuclear energy systems. The supplied review identifies provisions for defining the system, considering the complete cycle, analyzing pathways, documenting evidence and uncertainty, and assessing robustness, costs and verification. Its basic principle treats intrinsic features and extrinsic measures as essential complements, with neither sufficient alone. This is an established assessment framework, not a demonstration of the proposed innovation.

The IAEA's 2010 report, Technical Features to Enhance Proliferation Resistance of Nuclear Energy Systems, discusses civilian materials of concern, processing barriers, facility misuse and the relationship between intrinsic features and safeguards. It explicitly does not determine which complete systems or fuel cycles are superior or inferior to its reference light-water-reactor cycle in proliferation resistance. That qualification describes the scope of this report; it does not rule out comparative assessments made with explicit assumptions and methods.

The undated INPRO methodology overview describes the goal of reducing the attractiveness of nuclear materials and technology for weapons programmes while making diversion difficult and detectable. It also addresses lifecycle implementation and cost effectiveness. The supplied overview is a landing page rather than the complete methodology, and its statement that an updated manual was being finalized cannot establish the update's actual publication status at the assessment date.

The supplied review relied on truncated text from both technical PDFs; the 2010 report also had pages without extractable text. The visible passages support the specific principles summarized here, but the record does not justify treating either document as fully examined. The overview's extracted text was untruncated, although its substantive scope is narrower than the manuals. These limitations constrain the conclusions that can be drawn from the supplied evidence.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record contains no demonstration of a particular architecture meeting the proposed whole-cycle goal, and its bounded freshness search record is empty. The historical documents and undated overview do not establish whether a qualifying architecture remained undemonstrated as of 2026-11-01. No supported quantitative performance gains or economic results are available here. This is an unresolved limit of the record, not evidence that every proposed architecture has failed or that no subsequent progress occurred.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: define a complete fuel-cycle architecture, an explicit reference cycle and the threat scenarios against which improvement will be judged. Set thresholds in advance for what counts as substantially stronger proliferation resistance and economically credible operation. Assess lifecycle material flows, plausible acquisition and diversion pathways, facility misuse, and the limits of the architecture's influence on undeclared parallel activities. These are proposed completion criteria, not established IAEA thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Define complete fuel-cycle architecture with comparison baselines and advance thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: use independent assessment and representative facilities to test operational and safeguards claims. Report detection times and probabilities, measurement uncertainties, verification workload, costs and failure modes. Examine interactions among barriers, including whether defeating one also compromises others, and demonstrate compatibility with safety and security. Operational evidence should distinguish measured results from modeled projections and document the limits of extrapolation to a complete deployed cycle.
completion_criteria.label: Independently validate operational and safeguards claims using representative facilities

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: provide sufficient methods, assumptions and appropriately accessible evidence for independent assessors to reproduce the comparisons and evaluate sensitivity to uncertain inputs. Demonstrate that the claimed gains persist across a stated range of operating conditions, lifecycle stages and credible threat scenarios. A finite programme would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality. Completion would support a bounded claim of substantially improved resistance; the cycle should not be described as proliferation-proof.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce comparisons and demonstrate resistance gains within stated boundaries

completion_criteria.text: The rationale for these proposals comes from the INPRO emphasis on whole-cycle definition, pathway analysis, documented evidence, robustness, costs and verification, together with the IAEA's treatment of technical features and safeguards as complementary. Independent representative-facility validation and explicit improvement thresholds extend those principles into a proposed test of this innovation; the supplied sources do not establish them as a published consensus completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Identify INPRO and IAEA foundations without claiming consensus standards

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NUC-03, A scalable closed fuel cycle that consumes most long-lived actinides, has the closest material-flow overlap. Actinide consumption could contribute to inventory reduction, but its primary objective differs from demonstrating resistance across acquisition and diversion pathways. Closing a cycle or consuming actinides does not by itself establish NUC-13. NUC-05, Practical remote verification of otherwise inaccessible operating reactors, could contribute evidence for safeguards, but reactor verification covers only part of a complete fuel cycle. These distinctions follow from the supplied titles and descriptions; the full scopes of NUC-03 and NUC-05 were not supplied.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-09, Very-high-burnup fuel with robust fission-product retention, overlaps through fuel properties and material handling, while NUC-12, Reliable, non-invasive, real-time three-dimensional reactor-core diagnosis, overlaps through observability. Fuel retention and core diagnosis address different performance questions and would need separate assessment before their contribution to proliferation resistance could be established. NUC-08, Broadly applicable passive shutdown and long-term reactor cooling, addresses safety; compatibility with that objective matters, but passive safety does not demonstrate resistance to deliberate misuse.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-02, Mass-produced fission plants with radically lower delivered cost, and NUC-10, Long-lived, low-intervention nuclear power for remote sites, share deployment and operating constraints with NUC-13. Affordability, remote operation and limited intervention could shape safeguards implementation, but their achievement would not establish whole-cycle proliferation resistance. NUC-06, Reactor structural materials that remain reliable under extreme neutron exposure, and NUC-11, Durable materials and chemistry control for aggressive reactor coolants, concern reliability and materials performance that an integrated architecture may need, rather than its proliferation-resistance objective.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-01, A self-sustaining, net-electric fusion power plant, and NUC-07, Net-electric fusion using a low-neutron fuel cycle, concern fusion power production and neutron-related performance. Their titles alone establish no whole-cycle proliferation-resistance result. NUC-04, High-power nuclear propulsion for routine deep-space missions, concerns a propulsion application with a distinct operating context. Any relevant fuel-cycle resistance assessment would require that system's materials, facilities and lifecycle to be defined; achieving propulsion performance would not establish NUC-13.

brief.title: Nuclear power with stronger barriers to weapons misuse
possible: Countries could use nuclear power with a fuel system that makes obtaining material for weapons substantially harder and easier to detect. Protection would extend through fuel processing, transport, storage and disposal, with features that help inspectors check civilian use.
why: Fewer opportunities to acquire weapons material could strengthen confidence in civilian nuclear power. Easier detection could discourage misuse and give governments more opportunity to respond.

sources.showed: The agency described how material properties and facility design can impede weapons misuse and support inspections. Its report provides a framework, without ranking complete fuel systems.
sources.cited_for: Built-in protection and inspections must work together, and protective barriers must be assessed as a system.
sources.not_established: The report does not demonstrate a complete fuel system with substantially stronger protection against weapons misuse.

sources.who: International Atomic Energy Agency's INPRO project
sources.showed: INPRO developed an assessment framework covering the entire fuel system, routes to weapons material, interacting barriers, inspection arrangements and costs.
sources.quote:
INPRO developed a 
set of basic principles, user requirements a nd criteria together with  an assessment method
sources.cited_for: A credible comparison must examine the entire fuel system, its vulnerabilities, inspection needs and costs.
sources.not_established: An assessment framework does not establish that a particular fuel system achieves the proposed improvement.

shown: The International Atomic Energy Agency has developed ways to assess resistance to weapons misuse. These examine how technical barriers and safeguards—checks that nuclear activities remain civilian—work together. They establish assessment principles, rather than demonstrate the complete capability.
missing: A complete fuel system must demonstrate affordable protection without moving an easier route to weapons material elsewhere.
Tests in representative facilities must establish how reliably and quickly inspectors can detect misuse during normal operations.
Independent comparisons must establish that gains survive changing conditions and that defeating a barrier does not also defeat others.

milestones.label: A complete design with clear comparison rules
milestones.explanation: A complete fuel system would need a reference design, defined threats and advance thresholds for improvement and cost. These would establish what counts as success.

milestones.label: Independent facility tests confirm operating and inspection claims
milestones.explanation: Independent tests in representative facilities would have to measure detection performance, costs and failures alongside safe operation. This would test whether the proposed protections work in practice.

milestones.label: Independent comparisons reproduce gains across stated conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent assessors would have to reproduce comparisons and find lasting gains across defined conditions, stages and threats. This would establish the breadth of protection without claiming immunity to misuse.

milestones.label: Assessment foundations and proposed tests are clearly distinguished
milestones.explanation: The criteria would have to distinguish established IAEA assessment principles from the proposed thresholds and facility tests. This would clarify their basis without presenting them as agreed completion standards.

uncertain: How much improvement would count as substantial, and against which threats and reference fuel system?
Could the gains remain affordable while keeping inspection demands and civilian operations practical?
Built-in barriers cannot prevent an independent weapons programme; international cooperation and effective inspections would remain necessary.

page.title: Proliferation resistance by design in nuclear fuel cycles
page.definition: Civilian nuclear fuel cycles whose material, process and facility design makes diversion or misuse for weapons harder and more detectable than in a specified reference cycle. Built-in features operate across the life cycle alongside safeguards, the measures used to verify peaceful nuclear use.

goal.need: In 2024, IAEA safeguards required 14,776.5 days of field verification. The activity and equipment totals below show the verification system that fuel-cycle design must support. The IAEA identifies material and facility features that can impede misuse and assist safeguards; these figures do not establish a reduction in verification effort.

figures.caption: IAEA safeguards activities and equipment in 2024
rows: Surveillance cameras maintained at nuclear facilities
figures.note: These are safeguards totals, not measured benefits of a redesigned fuel cycle.

statements.body: International Atomic Energy Agency, International Project on Innovative Nuclear Reactors and Fuel Cycles
statements.quote: the attractiveness of nuclear materials and technology for diversion to a nuclear weapons programme should be low
statements.context: The passage states a requirement for innovative nuclear energy systems.

statements.quote: increase the assurance that they are a very unattractive and the least desirable route for diversion or theft of weapons-usable materials
statements.context: The subject is Generation IV nuclear energy systems. The complete goal also addresses physical protection.

completion.title: An operating fuel cycle demonstrates greater whole-cycle proliferation resistance than its reference.
completion.criterion: An operating civilian fuel cycle demonstrates greater difficulty and detectability of diversion and facility misuse than a specified operating reference cycle under the same stated threats. An independently peer-reviewed GIF proliferation-resistance comparison supports the whole-cycle improvement using operational evidence, including alternative acquisition paths, interacting barriers, uncertainty and verification costs. The system also meets INPRO requirements for pathway coverage, barrier robustness and an agreed safeguards approach. No numerical superiority margin is implied.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; qualitative synthesis of IAEA/INPRO requirements and the Generation IV International Forum goal.
completion.basis: Searches of IAEA NF-T-4.5, INPRO Volume 5, GIF PR&PP Revision 6 and the GIF roadmap found no universal superiority threshold or whole-cycle certification. INPRO accepts several attributes at parity with existing facilities. This Atlas test requires comparative improvement without assigning a percentage. The National Research Council records comparisons of once-through, partial actinide recycle and full actinide recycle fuel cycles.

milestones.title: A candidate fuel-cycle process works in tests at an appropriate scale.
milestones.criterion: The candidate's basic fuel-cycle flowsheet is established by testing at an appropriate scale, the GIF viability endpoint. A 2005 workshop contribution reports laboratory fabrication of 10 kg of spent pressurized-water-reactor fuel into DUPIC pellets and elements by 2002. DUPIC reuses this fuel in heavy-water reactors. This is component evidence for partial recycling, rather than qualification of a complete fuel cycle.
milestones.set_by: Generation IV International Forum, 2014 Technology Roadmap Update, Figure 1-2; an engineering endpoint published for Generation IV systems and their fuel-cycle technologies.

milestones.title: Candidate fuel-cycle processes work at a scale sufficient for a demonstration plant.
milestones.criterion: The candidate's engineering-scale processes are verified and optimised under prototypical conditions and validated at a scale sufficient for a demonstration plant. A 2009 peer-reviewed study reports an engineering-scale integrated processing test of Experimental Breeder Reactor-II spent fuel: four batches containing 50.4 kg of heavy metal. It establishes process performance, not whole-cycle proliferation resistance or qualification of the full-recycle class.
milestones.set_by: Generation IV International Forum, 2014 Technology Roadmap Update, Figure 1-2; a performance-phase engineering endpoint, not a proliferation-resistance pass mark.
milestones.threshold_quote: Processes validated at scale sufficient for demonstration plant.

milestones.title: Every facility of a candidate fuel cycle in a State has an agreed safeguards approach.
milestones.criterion: INPRO acceptance limit AL5.3 is met: every facility of the candidate system within a State is covered by a safeguards approach agreed with the verification authority. In 2007, the IAEA reported agreement on the basic safeguards systems and cost sharing for Japan's JMOX fuel-fabrication plant. That facility-level agreement is relevant to partial recycling but does not establish this whole-system milestone.
milestones.set_by: IAEA INPRO Manual—Proliferation Resistance, Volume 5, section 3.6.3, acceptance limit AL5.3.
milestones.threshold_quote: all facilities of the INS in a State are covered by an agreed safeguards approach.

milestones.title: A licensed prototype or demonstration fuel-cycle system operates.
milestones.criterion: The candidate's detailed design is complete and its prototype or demonstration system is licensed, constructed and operating. This is the operational engineering step before the whole-cycle comparison. GIF's December 2022 crosscutting report presents preliminary design information and qualitative assessments; it does not establish this milestone for an entire fuel-cycle class or demonstrate comparative whole-cycle superiority.
milestones.set_by: Generation IV International Forum, 2014 Technology Roadmap Update, demonstration-phase definition; an engineering endpoint for Generation IV systems, not certification of proliferation resistance.
milestones.threshold_quote: licensing, construction and operation of the system are carried out

not_found: No externally published numerical margin defining whole-cycle superiority in proliferation resistance was located.
No independently reviewed operational comparison meeting the completion test was located for any of the three fuel-cycle classes.
No proliferation-resistance-specific laboratory-to-operation qualification ladder was located; the engineering milestones come from the GIF development roadmap.
A final NG-T-3.26 proliferation-resistance manual was not located.
Two IAEA meeting PDFs concerning the INPRO revision returned HTTP 403.

results.finding: Five HTR-PM fuel spheres passed an irradiation test and achieved their expected performance.
results.detail: The irradiation test provides component evidence for the once-through fuel cycle; it does not establish the basic flowsheet through testing.
results.quote: The irradiation test of five fuel spheres of the HTR-PM started in October 2012 in the high flux reactor (HFR) in Petten, the Netherlands, and finished on December 30, 2014. As one of the key technologies in the HTR-PM project, the fuel spheres have been proved to achieve their expected performance.

results.finding: DUPIC fabrication: 10 kg of spent PWR fuel was made into fuel pellets and elements.
results.detail: This laboratory fabrication is component evidence for partial recycling; it does not establish the complete fuel-cycle flowsheet at an appropriate scale.
results.quote: From the start of this experiment until the year 2002 a total of 10 kg of spent PWR fuel that has undergone a nominal burn-up of 35,500 MWd/tU was fabricated into DUPIC fuel pellets and elements.

results.finding: EURO-GANEX recovered 99.9% of transuranium elements in a test using 116.8 g of irradiated fast-reactor fuel.
results.detail: The laboratory test demonstrated uranium and transuranium separation, a component of full actinide recycling. It did not establish a complete fuel-cycle flowsheet; the two extraction cycles were each run in separate steps.
results.quote:
TRU were recovered in the second cycle process with high efficiency (99.9%), together with only 0.06% of the 
lanthanides inventory and the major fraction of Zr and Mo.

results.finding: HTR-PM fuel manufacturing produced approximately 630,000 qualified spherical fuel elements by the end of 2018.
results.detail: Five elements underwent irradiation testing, but the text does not establish that the manufacturing process was optimized and validated under prototypical conditions. The article states that it has been retracted.
results.quote: By the end of 2018, the factory had already completed well-qualified production of approximately 630 000 spherical fuel elements.

results.finding: REMIX fuel: six lead-test assemblies entered pilot operation; three completed three 18-month cycles.
results.detail: The test reports reactor operating performance of recycled uranium-plutonium fuel. It does not establish verification and optimisation of the associated processing steps or their validation at demonstration-plant scale. Post-irradiation studies remain pending.
results.quote:
The third 18-month cycle of pilot industrial operation of REMIX fuel
assemblies has been successfully completed at Unit 1 of the Balakovo NPP, a
facility of Rosatom’s Electric Power Division.

results.finding: Engineering-scale integrated pyroprocessing test processed four batches of EBR-II spent fuel containing 50.4 kg of heavy metal.
results.detail: The test used fixed operating parameters and establishes process performance, not whole-cycle proliferation resistance or qualification of the full-recycle class.
results.quote: Four batches of the spent fuel (containing 50.4-kg heavy metal) were processed under a set of fixed operating parameters.

results.finding: Japan’s nuclear facilities: all facilities, number unspecified, had integrated safeguards approach coverage in January 2011.
results.detail: The report says coverage extended to all nuclear facilities and locations outside facilities. It separately states that the safeguards approach for the MOX fabrication plant under construction was being developed.
results.quote:
To deal with the broad range of nuclear facilities and LOFs in Japan, the application 
of the Integrated Safeguards Approaches was expanded in a stepwise manner and reached full 
coverage of all nuclear facilities and LOFs in Japan in January 2011.

results.finding: DUPIC fuel fabrication processed 10 kg of spent PWR fuel into pellets and elements.
results.detail: The work used hot-cell experiments and research-reactor irradiation. The text does not establish engineering-scale optimization or validation at a scale sufficient for a demonstration plant.
results.quote: From the start of this experiment until the year 2002 a total of 10 kg of spent PWR fuel that has undergone a nominal burn-up of 35,500 MWd/tU was fabricated into DUPIC fuel pellets and elements.

results.finding: EURO-GANEX processed 116.8 g of irradiated fuel pieces; second-cycle transuranium recovery was 99.9%.
results.detail: The fuel mass included cladding. The hot test demonstrated a candidate separation process, but the text does not establish engineering-scale validation sufficient for a demonstration plant; process optimisation remained ongoing.
results.quote:
TRU were recovered in the second cycle process with high efficiency (99.9%), together with only 0.06% of the 
lanthanides inventory and the major fraction of Zr and Mo.

results.finding: HTR-PM fuel fabrication: approximately 630,000 spherical elements produced by the end of 2018.
results.detail: Fuel fabrication is a component of a candidate cycle; the report does not establish its complete flowsheet. The article has been retracted.
results.quote: By the end of 2018, the factory had already completed well-qualified production of approximately 630 000 spherical fuel elements.

results.finding: One HTR-PM demonstration nuclear power plant had entered commissioning.
results.detail: The plant was under construction and commissioning, not operating; the article does not establish an operating demonstration fuel-cycle system. The article has been retracted.
results.quote: A 200 MWe demonstration HTGR NPP project (HTR-PM) is currently under construction and has entered the phase of engineering commissioning in Shidao Bay, Rongcheng City, Shandong Province.

results.finding: Six REMIX lead-test assemblies completed three 18-month fuel cycles.
results.detail: The reactor test provides component evidence for recycling recovered uranium and plutonium, but does not establish the basic flowsheet of a complete fuel cycle.
results.quote:
The assemblies have undergone a standard
operational fuel life for Russian VVER-1000 reactors — three 18-month fuel
cycles, thus completing the LTA program.

results.finding: Six REMIX lead-test assemblies entered pilot operation; the last three completed three 18-month cycles.
results.detail: The release reports operation of fuel assemblies in an existing reactor, not a licensed, constructed and operating prototype or demonstration of the complete fuel-cycle system.
results.quote:
The assemblies have undergone a standard
operational fuel life for Russian VVER-1000 reactors — three 18-month fuel
cycles, thus completing the LTA program.

results.finding: An engineering-scale pyroprocessing test processed four batches of spent breeder fuel containing 50.4 kg of heavy metal.
results.detail: The test demonstrated processing and uranium recovery, but the excerpt does not establish the basic flowsheet for a complete fuel cycle.
results.quote: Four batches of the spent fuel (containing 50.4-kg heavy metal) were processed under a set of fixed operating parameters.

results.finding: Liquid cadmium cathode recovery: 3 experiments collected 1–2 kg of heavy metal each.
results.detail: The experiments tested an electrorefining step using spent reactor fuel and detected transuranic actinides in the recovered material. They do not establish a complete full-actinide-recycle flowsheet.
results.quote: In the three experiments performed to date, between 1 and 2 kg of heavy metal was collected in the LCC after passing an integrated current between 1.80 and 2.16 MC (500 and 600 A h) from the anode to the cathode.
